name: Forty Floors and Falling (No One Catches)
description:
Released in 2201 by Tariqe Mensah-Volkov, a former Tier 2 maintenance worker who lost his left arm to an industrial accident and received no corporate compensation, 'Forty Floors and Falling (No One Catches)' is the defining protest anthem of the post-Collapse labor movement. Built on a foundation of West African kpanlogo rhythms played on salvaged steel drums, layered with a mournful Mongolian throat-singing drone and a guitar line that sounds like a body hitting scaffolding, the song documents the experience of falling — literally and economically — through the tiers. Mensah-Volkov's voice is rough, unpolished, and devastating, and the song's central hook, 'Forty floors and falling / and the Spire don't even look down,' became graffiti on every maintenance corridor in the Circuit within weeks of the song's pirate-feed release.

Vantablack Media's legal division issued three successive takedown orders, each of which only amplified the song's reach through encrypted mesh networks and bootleg data chips sold on the Shelf. The song's second verse, which names specific Vantablack executives and details the actuarial formulas corporations use to calculate acceptable worker casualties, is the section most often cited in the ban orders. In 2203, when dockworkers at the Lake Michigan logistics hub staged a seventeen-day strike, they played this song on loop from a solar-powered speaker lashed to a crane for the duration of the action. It has since become standard at labor organizing meetings, memorial services for workplace casualties, and any gathering where someone needs to remember why they're angry.
creator: Tariqe Mensah-Volkov
genre: Shelf protest, labor folk, polyrhythm steel
audience: Tier 1 and Tier 2 workers, labor organizers, maintenance crews, dockworkers, anyone who has been hurt by a corporation and received nothing
cultural_impact: The song functionally catalyzed the 2203 dockworkers' strike and is credited by labor historians with reviving collective action culture in the Circuit after two decades of suppression. Corporate security firms have standing orders to confiscate data chips containing the song. The phrase 'the Spire don't even look down' has entered everyday speech as shorthand for institutional indifference to lower-tier suffering. Mensah-Volkov himself disappeared in 2204 under circumstances that were officially ruled a 'voluntary relocation' but are widely understood as corporate disappearance, which has made him a martyr figure and the song untouchable in terms of cultural weight.
known_fans: anyone who lost a limb or a family member to an industrial accident
story_hooks: A player character finds a data chip with the song on a dead body in a maintenance tunnel — the chip also contains something else, a second file hidden in the audio's metadata, that someone clearly killed to keep quiet.

The players are hired to locate Tariqe Mensah-Volkov, officially listed as relocated, by someone who claims to be his daughter — and the trail leads somewhere a corporation very much does not want them to go.

A labor action is building to a flashpoint and the organizers need someone to publicly perform the song at a rally, knowing that doing so will immediately bring corporate security attention — they're asking the players to provide protection.
